Featured project

Daily schedules for stylists, sent automatically

Intro Shop offers styling sessions with five specialists. Every day this Zap pulls tomorrow’s bookings from the shop’s booking table, works out who is seeing whom, applies VIP pricing and posts a separate schedule for each specialist to the shop’s Telegram orders group. Nobody has to copy booking details by hand.

TriggerRuns every daySchedule by Zapier
FindTomorrow’s bookings pulledFormatter and Zapier Tables
ProcessSchedules built per specialistCode by Zapier (JavaScript)
DeliverOne message per specialistLooping by Zapier and Telegram

Messy input, handled in codeZapier passes the found records as comma-separated strings, but specialist names contain commas too. The code matches names against a list of known specialists instead of splitting blindly.

Business rules built inVIP clients get 15% off. Duplicate rows are removed, bookings are filtered to the next day and sorted by time.

One message per personA loop sends each specialist’s schedule as its own message, so everyone sees only their bookings.

Booking intake with pricing and routing

Tally, then Zapier Tables and Storage by Zapier, then AI by Zapier, then Paths, then Zapier Tables or Gmail

This is where every Intro Shop styling booking starts. Each Tally submission is saved as a record, and Storage by Zapier keeps count of how many services each client has booked. AI by Zapier calculates the booking price, then Paths check the count: clients who have booked more than three services become VIPs and get 15% off, and clients receive a confirmation email with their booking details and price.

The same table feeds the daily stylist schedules in the featured project. I also built intake versions with Typeform and Zapier Forms.

AI sentiment analysis for customer feedback

Typeform or Google Forms, then AI by Zapier, then Paths, then Google Sheets

Every feedback response is read by AI and labeled Positive, Neutral, Negative or Mixed, using a structured prompt with examples. Paths then route each group differently, so negative feedback is never buried in a spreadsheet.

IP address extraction and location lookup

Gmail, then AI by Zapier, then Google Sheets, then Webhooks (IP geolocation API)

When a matching email arrives, AI by Zapier reads the email headers and pulls out the IP address, which is logged in a Google Sheet. A webhook then sends that IP to a geolocation API to find where it comes from.

My first version found nothing, because the IP address is in the email header, not the body. I rewrote the AI prompt to look in the right place and mapped its output into the API request, so the value changes with every email.

Schedule, then Formatter and Zapier Tables, then Formatter, then Telegram

Once a month this Zap works out which month to report on, finds that month’s bookings in the shop’s table, adds up the prices and posts the total to the shop’s Telegram orders group. The owner gets the month’s revenue without opening a spreadsheet.

Bulk price calculation across the booking table

Make

Repairing and finishing a lead cleanup scenario

JSON, then Iterator, then Set variables, then If-else and Merge, then filter, then Text aggregator, then Gmail

A sales team’s leads from Instagram, the website and Telegram arrived in a mess: random capital letters, stray spaces in emails, phone numbers written every possible way. I took over a half-built Make scenario from a previous automator, found the bugs in the existing modules, added the missing ones and finished it, so the manager gets one tidy email listing every lead.

Names are trimmed and capitalized, emails lowercased, and sources mapped to one of four values. Phone numbers go through an If-else with three branches, one per format, and Merge brings them back together as +380XXXXXXXXX. A filter drops leads with no way to contact them. While testing, I traced why a lead with no contacts still reached the email: the fallback text was only added after the filter, so the filter saw an empty value instead. Moving it earlier fixed it.

n8n

Used-laptop deal scanner for resellers

Two workflows: Loop Over Items with Apify and Code, then an n8n Data Table; then Data Table, Code, OpenAI with structured output, a second loop with Apify, Code, Sort, Limit and Telegram

A reseller makes money by buying used laptops below market price and selling them on. To spot a good deal you first need to know what the market price is, so I split the job into two workflows that share one table.

The price base loops through five laptop models, collects up to 100 OLX listings for each through an Apify scraper and cleans them in JavaScript: wrong models, spare parts, iCloud-locked laptops, cases, new items and listings without a price are dropped, and dollar prices are converted to hryvnias. What’s left is saved to an n8n Data Table.

The scanner runs every day at noon. It works out the median and price range for each model from that table, asks OpenAI to suggest a resale price, a quick-sale discount, a minimum margin and a “suspiciously cheap” threshold, then checks fresh listings and sends the ten most profitable deals to Telegram, best first.

Workflow 1 · Price base

TriggerRun on demandManual trigger
Collect5 models, up to 100 listings eachLoop Over Items and Apify
CleanRight model, working, used, pricedCode (JavaScript)
StoreOne row per listingn8n Data Table

Workflow 2 · Deal scanner

TriggerEvery day at 12:00Schedule Trigger
BenchmarkMedian and price range per modelData Table and Code
AISuggest resale price and thresholdsOpenAI, limited by code
ScanProfit, margin and ROI per lotLoop, Apify and Code
DeliverTop 10 deals, best firstSort, Limit and Telegram

Code calculates, AI judgesEvery number (median, profit, margin) is calculated in code. The AI only suggests parameters, and code keeps them within safe limits: the resale price can never go above the market median, the discount stays between 0 and 15%, the minimum margin between 8 and 30%.

Whole-word matchingModel filters match separate words only, so “Legion 5” doesn’t pick up a “15IKB” or “512 GB” listing, and a MacBook Air M1 search drops M2, M3 and Pro models.

Never stops halfwayIf the scraper fails for one model, that model is skipped and the loop moves on. Without a scraper key the scanner switches to demo listings, and without AI it uses default settings.

How one deal is scored

Market price19,000 ₴
Sell price (−5% for a quick sale)18,050 ₴
Costs (2% fee + 300 ₴ prep)661 ₴
Listing price14,000 ₴
Profit3,389 ₴Margin 18.8% · ROI 24.2%

A deal is sent only if profit is at least 1,500 ₴ and the margin clears the model’s minimum. Listings priced far below market are skipped as likely scams or hidden defects. I use the median rather than the average because a few extreme listings, a sealed new laptop or one sold for parts, would pull the average away from the real market price. Course assignment at DAN.IT; the prices are asking prices, as OLX doesn’t publish actual sales.

RAG customer chatbot for a sports club chain

n8n Form, then OpenAI embeddings, then MongoDB Atlas Vector Search; Telegram, then AI Agent with retrieval and MongoDB memory, then Telegram

A case study for EnerGym, a chain of sports clubs: a Telegram bot that answers members’ questions from the club’s own documents and takes membership applications and training bookings. Staff upload PDFs such as prices, the timetable and pool rules through an n8n form. The workflow embeds them with OpenAI and stores them in a MongoDB Atlas vector store.

Each Telegram message goes to an AI Agent (gpt-4o-mini) that searches that knowledge base before it answers, so it quotes real prices and times instead of inventing them. MongoDB chat memory remembers each person’s last 10 messages. I wrote the agent’s instructions to ask one question at a time, check the phone number format, turn “tomorrow” or “on Monday” into an exact date in the club’s time zone, and flag complaints, refund requests and unanswered questions for a manager.

Order stock check with branded confirmation emails

Webhook, then Code, then Loop Over Items with Google Sheets and If, then Code, then If, then Gmail

When a customer places an order on the Intro Shop website, a webhook sends the order to n8n. JavaScript splits it into individual items, and a loop checks each one against the stock sheet in Google Sheets, logging the result. When every item has been checked, the workflow decides which email to send.

If everything is in stock, the customer gets a confirmation with their order. If something is short, they get a different email listing the missing pieces and their options: ship what’s ready, swap a size or style, or cancel at no charge. Both emails are styled HTML that matches the shop’s brand.

AI-curated morning news digests

Schedule, then Split Out and RSS Read, then Code (JavaScript), then an LLM chain with structured JSON output, then Filter, then Code, then Telegram

Every morning at 9:00, n8n reads a list of news sources I choose, keeps only items from the last 24 hours, removes duplicates and sends each article to OpenAI. The AI returns structured JSON: a short headline, a one-sentence summary, an importance score from 1 to 10 and an emoji. Only articles scoring 6 or higher make it into one tidy Telegram message, with the most important at the top.

I run two versions from the same design, changing only the settings node: one follows AI and automation news, the other follows official UK and US immigration sources (GOV.UK, USCIS and the Federal Register). Everything configurable (sources, topic, time window, how many items reach the AI and the digest) lives in one settings node, so a new digest takes minutes to set up.

TriggerEvery day at 9:00Schedule Trigger
CollectRead every chosen sourceSplit Out and RSS Read
CleanLast 24 hours, no duplicatesCode (JavaScript)
AISummarise and score 1–10OpenAI, structured JSON
DeliverTop stories in one messageFilter, Code and Telegram

Built for reliability: if one source is down the others still run, and on quiet days the bot still sends a short “nothing important today” message instead of failing silently.

Exchange rate bot with a three-level fallback

Settings, then HTTP Request (National Bank of Ukraine), then If, then a backup HTTP Request, then If, then a stored value, then Telegram

A Telegram bot that sends the USD exchange rate and is built to deliver a message every time, even when its data sources fail. Plan A asks the National Bank of Ukraine. If that request fails or returns an empty answer, plan B asks a backup API. If both fail, plan C uses the last known rate from the settings node.

Each request retries twice before giving up, and an If node checks that the rate is a real number, because an API can answer “200 OK” with no data. The message always names its source, and when the stored rate is used it warns that the figure may be out of date. I tested all four scenarios with switches that deliberately break each source.

Plan ANational Bank of UkraineHTTP Request with retry
Plan BBackup exchange rate APIRuns on error or empty data
Plan CLast known rateFlagged as possibly out of date
DeliverRate, date and sourceTelegram

Form validation with error handling

n8n Form, then Code (JavaScript), then an HTTP Request to a phone validation API, or a Telegram alert on error

When someone submits a form, a JavaScript Code node checks the phone number. If the format is wrong, for example a missing country code, the node fails on purpose and n8n sends the item down its error output: the team gets a Telegram alert saying what went wrong and who submitted it, and the workflow doesn’t crash. Numbers that pass go on to AbstractAPI, which checks whether the number is real.

For failures I can’t predict, such as the API being down, the workflow settings link a separate error workflow. If the main workflow crashes, that error workflow runs and sends an alert with the workflow name, the error message and the node that failed.
